issues.legal_issue: In a complaint case involving an offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session, the magistrate must apply a preliminary threshold and must not meticulously assess the evidence as if conducting a trial.
material_facts: The complaint alleged offences exclusively triable by the Court of Session.
At the preliminary inquiry, the complainant and witnesses stated that the accused had shot the complainant and caused the fatal shooting of another person.
The magistrate rejected the allegations after extensively assessing the evidence.
issues.conclusion: There was prima facie evidence against the accused that required consideration by the Court of Session; the magistrate erred by dismissing the complaint against him after a meticulous appraisal of the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 200, 202, 203 and 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the magistrate must determine on a cursory perusal whether sufficient ground exists to proceed, not weigh evidence as at trial. For an offence exclusively triable by the Court of Session, prima facie evidence is sufficient to issue process and commit the case; Sections 209 and 227 provide for commitment and for discharge by the Sessions Judge where sufficient ground to proceed is absent. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh.

predicates.complaint_case_exclusively_sessions: The proceeding began with a complaint alleging an offence triable exclusively by the Court of Session.
predicates.preliminary_evidence_supports_accusation: The material gathered in the preliminary inquiry provides prima facie support for the accusation against the person concerned.
predicates.magistrate_meticulously_weighed_evidence: The magistrate assessed the preliminary evidence in detail as though deciding the case at trial.

issues.definition: When a complaint alleging an offence exclusively triable by the Court of Session is supported by prima facie evidence, a magistrate who has meticulously weighed that evidence should issue process and commit the case.

issues.legal_issue: Connected criminal cases arising from the same transaction should ordinarily be tried separately by the same court to reduce the risk of conflicting findings.
material_facts: A complaint case and a police case arose from the same transaction.
The account in the complaint concerning a death was likely to be the complainant’s defence in the police case, which was pending before the Court of Session.
issues.conclusion: It was ordinarily desirable that the two cases be tried separately but by the same court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the practice of having connected cross-cases arising from the same transaction tried separately by the same court to avoid inconsistent findings, relying on Bannappa, AIR 1944 Bom 146; Judhister, 27 Cal WN 700; AIR 1923 Cal 644; and Periaswami, 1937 Mad WN 998.

predicates.connected_criminal_cases: Two criminal proceedings are connected because they concern opposing accounts of the same events.
predicates.same_transaction: The proceedings arise from the same transaction.
predicates.conflicting_findings_risk: Different courts deciding the proceedings could reach inconsistent findings.

issues.definition: When connected criminal cases arise from the same transaction and separate courts risk inconsistent findings, separate trials by the same court are ordinarily desirable.

issues.legal_issue: The extraordinary jurisdiction to review a criminal order is not to be used to correct every error where the error has not caused a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The magistrate’s excessive assessment of evidence was an error in the exercise of jurisdiction, rather than a lack of inherent jurisdiction.
The Court considered the complainant’s account of the fatal shooting highly improbable and noted that the complainant had been acquitted in the connected case.
The Court found that the magistrate’s error had not caused a gross failure of justice.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to interfere under Article 136 and dismissed the petition.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 does not create a general right of appeal or make the Supreme Court a general court of review for every error of law or fact in a criminal case. Its extraordinary power is reserved for exceptional cases where the error below has caused a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice.

rule.if: special_leave_criminal_proceeding and lower_court_error and not grave_substantial_miscarriage

predicates.special_leave_criminal_proceeding: The proceeding asks the Supreme Court to exercise extraordinary review of a criminal order.
predicates.lower_court_error: A court below committed an error in deciding or handling the proceeding.
predicates.grave_substantial_miscarriage: The error caused a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: In an extraordinary review of a criminal order, a lower-court error without a grave and substantial miscarriage of justice does not warrant interference.

issues.legal_issue: A complaint may be dismissed against persons where the preliminary inquiry provides no ground to proceed against them.
material_facts: The complaint accused public revenue officials of making false reports and assisting or abetting offences.
The magistrate’s inquiry disclosed no evidence that the officials had made false reports or abetted an offence.
The Supreme Court also held that the dismissal against the land allottees was unassailable.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal of the complaint against the revenue officials and the allottees was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 202 and 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the magistrate may dismiss a complaint where the preliminary inquiry discloses no sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused.

predicates.complaint_preliminary_inquiry: The proceeding is a complaint in which the magistrate has conducted a preliminary inquiry.
predicates.no_evidence_supporting_accusation_agains: The preliminary inquiry reveals no evidence supporting the accusation against the person concerned.

issues.definition: When a complaint preliminary inquiry reveals no evidence supporting an accusation against a person, the complaint may be dismissed as to that person.
